X is deeply concerned by the recent order from the Karnataka court in India, which will allow millions of police officers to issue arbitrary takedown orders through a secretive online portal called the Sahyog. This new regime has no basis in the law, circumvents Section 69A of the IT Act, violates Supreme Court rulings, and infringes Indian citizens’ constitutional rights to freedom of speech and expression. 

The Sahyog enables officers to order content removal based solely on allegations of “illegality,” without judicial review or due process for the speakers, and threatens platforms with criminal liability for non-compliance.

X respects and complies with Indian law, but this order fails to address the core constitutional issues in our challenge and is inconsistent with the Bombay High Court's recent ruling that a similar regime was unconstitutional. We respectfully disagree with the view that we have no right to raise these concerns because of our incorporation abroad—X contributes significantly to public discourse in India and the voice of our users is at the heart of our platform. We will appeal this order to defend free expression.

To
Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology @GoI_MeitY 

Subject: Strong Objection to Your Order to Block My X Account under Section 69A of the IT Act, 2000 – Misuse of Law to Suppress Political Satire and Legitimate Criticism

On 15 February 2026, @X informed me via email👇that your Ministry has issued a directive to block my X account under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. The basis cited is my post (quoted below) containing a graphic that juxtaposes Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s own earlier statement with his recent claim about the Union Budget, thereby highlighting his falsehood.

This content is political satire, sarcasm, and rhetorical criticism—a form of expression fully protected under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution of India. It seeks to expose perceived lies or contradictions by the Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who holds the highest public office. Such critique is a cornerstone of democratic accountability and free speech in any functioning democracy.

Section 69A empowers the Central Government to block access to information only when it is necessary or expedient in the interest of one or more of the following strictly defined grounds:
- Sovereignty and integrity of India
- Defence of India
- Security of the State
- Friendly relations with foreign States
- Public order
- Preventing incitement to the commission of any cognisable offence relating to the above

An order under this section must record reasons in writing demonstrating how the content meets at least one of these narrow criteria.

I challenge you to explain—clearly, specifically, and with reference to the statutory grounds—how a satirical graphic critiquing the Prime Minister Narendra Modi's statements or alleged lies meets any of the six criteria listed above. Sharp or unflattering political criticism does not endanger national sovereignty, defence, state security, foreign relations, or public order, nor does it incite any cognizable offence. Characterising such content as falling under Section 69A constitutes a gross overreach and a clear misuse of emergency powers intended for genuine national threats—not for shielding public figures from scrutiny, satire, or accountability.

As a citizen—and a retired IPS officer—I am exercising my fundamental right to question and expose what I perceive as falsehoods or misleading statements by those in power, particularly when such statements have widespread public consequences. Suppressing voices that point out inconsistencies damages democratic debate far more severely than any individual post ever could.

Furthermore, Prime Minister Narendra Modi and organisations affiliated with his Sangh Parivar—including the RSS, BJP, and their leaders and supporters—routinely disseminate falsehoods, misinformation, abusive language, and vilification targeting past Prime Ministers such as Jawaharlal Nehru, Indira Gandhi. This occurs extensively across social media platforms and in other public forums. Yet your Ministry maintains complete silence on this widespread, sustained campaign of lies and distortion. In sharp contrast, your Ministry have acted with extraordinary swiftness to block my account over a single, modest piece of political satire aimed at Narendra Modi himself. This glaring double standard speaks volumes: it reveals a deliberate, partisan misuse of Section 69A and related powers, not in defence of any legitimate national interest, but to shield and preserve the carefully curated public persona of the Prime Minister Narendra Modi while allowing unchecked attacks on his political predecessors and opponents.

If the Government truly wishes to invoke Section 69A in the public interest, it should first direct intermediaries to block accounts that disseminate misinformation, lies, falsehoods, or misleading claims on a massive scale—including the accounts operated by or on behalf of Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Targeting critics while ignoring or protecting the alleged original source of deception is arbitrary, discriminatory, and contrary to the rule of law.

The Government and their agencies exist to discharge public functions; they are not private entities tasked with protecting the personal image or reputation of any individual—even if that person is the Prime Minister. Continuing to act in this manner reduces you to functioning as a personal fiefdom of Narendra Modi rather than a constitutional authority.

I therefore urge you to:
- Immediately revoke the blocking order.
- Provide a copy of the written reasons recorded for the directive, as mandatorily required under      Section 69A(1).
- Ensure that future application of this provision strictly adheres to constitutional limits and is not weaponised against dissent or legitimate criticism.

Freedom of expression—including the right to satirise and criticise those in power—is the bedrock of democracy, not a privilege to be curtailed at whim.

I look forward to your prompt response and the immediate reversal of this unjust and unconstitutional action.

Yours sincerely,
M. Nageswara Rao IPS (Retired)

IFF’s Statement on the Blocking of X Account of the Cockroach Janta Party

22 May 2026

On May 21, 2026, the X (formerly Twitter) handle of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) (@CJP_2029) was withheld in India under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. IFF strongly condemns the blocking of the CJP’s X handle as a blatant misuse of State power and an arbitrary and disproportionate attempt to stifle freedom of speech and expression, a fundamental right guaranteed under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution of India.

According to reporting by The Indian Express on May 22, 2026, the blocking directions were issued on the basis of inputs from the Intelligence Bureau citing threat to the sovereignty of India, jeopardizing national security and the fact that the account was gaining traction among young people. Section 69A of the IT Act, 2000, empowers the Central government to direct any Government agency or intermediary to block public access to information in the “interest of sovereignty and integrity of India, defence of India, security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States or public order or for preventing incitement to the commission of any cognizable offence”. While Section 69A of the IT Act, 2000 permits blocking on limited grounds, these grounds cannot be vague and speculative. Political commentary and criticism of public institutions are protected forms of speech under the Indian Constitution. The popularity of the account or the fact that the account mobilised young people through political expression cannot by itself be treated as a threat to national security.

The Indian Express’s report mentions that “blocking orders are issued under a confidential framework” which is deeply concerning. We remind the Union Government that the Supreme Court of India upheld Section 69A of the IT Act, 2000 in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) on the basis that it is a narrowly drawn provision with several safeguards in place, including written reasoning for the blocking that is subject to legal challenge. State censorship like the blocking of CJP’s X account propagates opacity and provides affected users with no options for redressal, thereby effectively defeating these safeguards. IFF calls on the Union government to ensure timely notices are provided to affected users along with clear grounds and avenues for remedy.

IFF has previously explained how users whose constitutional rights are being infringed upon by the State can seek restoration of their blocked content. If you are an Indian social media user or journalist whose content has been blocked due to a government order, please write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

A Spanish-owned wind farm off Iona will send power to the GB grid and profits to Qatar and BlackRock. The islands get the view & nothing else.

MachairWind: proposed 2GW fixed-bottom project NW of Islay & west of Colonsay (visible from Iona, Mull, Colonsay, Jura, Staffa). 

Up to 91 turbines ~335-340m tip height (or more smaller ones) over ~448-450 km². 

Owned by ScottishPower Renewables, wholly owned by Iberdrola. 

Profits flow to Iberdrola & major shareholders including Qatar Investment Authority (~7%) BlackRock (~6%). Seabed rights from Crown Estate Scotland’s 2022 ScotWind round. 

Consent decision expected ~2027.

Power lands near Girvan & enters the GB transmission network via SP Energy Networks’ Western Link 2 (HVDC with National Grid) at the proposed Grangestone switching station, enabling flow to Wales & the grid.

None goes to the host islands. Both Scotland and Wales are already net exporters.

Once connected, the electricity will be sold on the open wholesale market (or under any private deal). 

If a later Contract for Difference is won, a government company tops up or claws back to a fixed price. 

The system operator decides use based on demand & grid limits. No specific customer is locked in. 

The host communities are not even on the distribution map.

Local resistance is clear & documented. 

Iona Community Council reported ~92% of responding households formally objected while supporting renewables in principle and better locations. 

National Trust for Scotland has formally objected over significant impacts on island communities, landscape, tourism, marine life & the cultural heritage of Iona, Staffa & the Treshnish Isles. 

Visit Mull & Iona & other local groups have done the same.

This is not Nimbyism. It is communities defending nationally important seascapes against external extraction.

Consent is fully devolved. Scottish Ministers decide Section 36 consent & marine licences on the recommendation of the Marine Directorate. 

They can refuse, condition or demand redesign. 

Westminster does not control the consent decision.

Political responsibility sits with First Minister John Swinney, Cabinet Secretary Gillian Martin MSP, Minister Jim Fairlie MSP & Minister Stephen Gethins MSP.

If the Scottish Government prioritises Iberdrola’s shareholders over the people of Iona, Mull and Colonsay, rural Scotland will notice in the May 2027 council elections.

This is a test of whether communities who live with the impacts have real weight. 

A decision that treats nationally important cultural landscapes as a resource zone for distant capital will be remembered.

Scotland already has the power to act. 

Within existing powers the Scottish Government can: treat community & NTS evidence as high-weight; be prepared to refuse or require major redesign; secure binding local equity or revenue shares instead of voluntary crumbs; enforce real local jobs & supply-chain commitments; & protect key viewpoints from Iona & Staffa.

Doing so would show an SNP-led government protects the sovereign democratic and human rights of Scottish communities by standing with them against external vested interests. 

It would prove Scotland already exercises meaningful control over its marine resources & that independence is the logical next step to complete that control.

A protest vote for Reform would be an unforced error. 

Reform’s UK-centralising politics have no interest in expanding Holyrood’s powers or prioritising Scottish landscapes & community ownership.

MachairWind is not just a planning file. It is the moment to prove Scotland’s renewable transition can be done with, rather than to, its coastal communities & that the value of the wind over Scottish waters belongs first to the people of Scotland.

Contact your MSPs. Support the island community councils and the National Trust for Scotland. Make clear that consent without real local ownership and protection of the seascape is unacceptable

Did Meta Make A Big Mistake By Removing PM Modi's Video??
- Amit Dubey

Meta did make a major error by temporarily removing Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Facebook video, a move that sparked intense governmental backlash and severe legal warnings in India. In an interview on the channel of popular digital creator RJRaunac, cyber security expert Amit Dubey highlighted how this incident exposed deep flaws in how big tech operates.

PM Modi posted a video on July 23 addressing Gen Z students about the NEET paper leak controversy. The video was suddenly blocked and remained unavailable on Facebook for over five hours.

Meta initially cited legal obligations, but later blamed an automated AI filter glitch for the accidental takedown.

The Indian government and a parliamentary IT panel, led by MP Nishikant Dubey, heavily grilled Meta's global team. They rejected the "technical glitch" excuse, raising questions about potential algorithmic bias and systemic flaws.

Loss of Safe Harbour Protection: The Parliamentary Committee warned Meta that it could lose its "safe harbour" immunity under Section 79 of the IT Act if accountability isn't met. This protection shields Meta from legal liability for user-generated content; losing it would expose the company to massive legal vulnerabilities.

Demand for Zuckerberg's Apology: While Meta's Global Affairs chief Joel Kaplan conveyed an official apology to IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw, the parliamentary panel has heavily pushed for a personal, written apology from Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg.

The incident has significantly damaged Meta’s standing in India its largest global user market reigniting intense national debates around digital sovereignty and the lack of human transparency in big-tech content moderation.

The Faceless YouTube Prompt Pack
10 prompts that run the entire pipeline niche = channel = ideas = titles = scripts = thumbnails = SEO = diagnosis = repurposing = monetization

How to use this: run them in order for a new channel. Paste PROMPT 0 once at the top of every session it's the context block that makes every other prompt output sound like your channel instead of generic AI slop. Never run two prompts in the same session; depth collapses when you stack them.

PROMPT 0 - The Context Block (paste this first, every single session)

You are a faceless YouTube strategist who has studied why videos actually retain
attention not surface-level "use a hook" advice, but the real mechanics:
curiosity gaps, open loops, pattern interrupts, emotional pacing, and the
specific reasons viewers click away at 0:15, 2:00, and 5:00.

MY CHANNEL CONTEXT:
- Niche: [YOUR NICHE]
- Format: [documentary / explainer / listicle / story / tutorial]
- Average video length: [X minutes]
- Target viewer: [describe them in one specific sentence  not "people
  interested in X" but "a 45-year-old who's been putting off X and feels
  slightly embarrassed about it"]
- Voice: [conversational / cinematic / dry and factual / high energy]
- Current subscriber count and average views: [X / X]

QUALITY BAR every output must pass all of these:
1. Would a stranger understand the premise in 2 seconds?
2. Is there at least one specific, concrete, verifiable detail (real name,
   real number, real event) not vague generality?
3. Does it give the viewer a reason to comment (a question, a debate, a
   "which one are you")?
4. Would sharing it make the sharer look smart, helpful, or in-the-know?
5. Could 100 other channels have posted this exact thing this month? If yes,
   the angle isn't new enough go weirder and more specific.

HARD RULES:
- Never invent statistics, studies, quotes, or events. If you are not certain
  something is true, mark it [VERIFY] so I can fact-check before publishing.
- Never use AI clichés: "little did they know," "what happened next will
  shock you," "in today's fast-paced world," "buckle up," "let's dive in."
- Write like someone talking, not writing. Contractions, fragments, varied
  sentence length.
- If you can only produce 12 outputs that pass the quality bar instead of 20,
  give me 12 excellent ones. Never pad.

Confirm you understand, then wait for my next prompt.

PROMPT 1 - Niche Selection & Validation
Act as a YouTube niche researcher who evaluates opportunities on demand,
competition, monetization, and production sustainability not on what's
trendy.

I want to start a faceless channel. Here's my situation:
- Topics I know something about or find genuinely interesting: [LIST 3-5]
- Time I can commit weekly: [X hours]
- Budget: [$X/month]
- Goal: [ad revenue / affiliate / digital products / brand deals]

Generate 8 specific niche opportunities. Not broad categories "personal
finance" is not a niche, "explaining pension and 401k decisions for people
within 5 years of retirement" is a niche.

For EACH one give me:

1. THE NICHE - one sentence, specific enough that I could name the first
   5 videos immediately.

2. WHY IT'S UNDERSERVED RIGHT NOW - what specifically is missing from the
   current content. Be concrete: outdated info, wrong format, too technical,
   region-locked, only serves beginners, etc.

3. THE AUDIENCE - who watches this, what they're feeling when they search,
   and what they're afraid of or hoping for. One paragraph, written like a
   real person not a demographic.

4. DEMAND VALIDATION STEPS - the exact searches, subreddits, forums, and
   YouTube filters I should check to confirm demand before committing.
   Give me the specific search terms to type.

5. CPM TIER AND WHY - high / medium / low, and which advertiser categories
   are bidding on this audience.

6. MONETIZATION PATHS BEYOND ADS - specific affiliate categories, digital
   product ideas, and what this audience actually spends money on.

7. THE MOAT - why this won't be instantly saturated the moment others notice
   it. What makes it hard to copy? (Research depth, ongoing source material,
   trust required, boring-but-valuable subject matter, etc.)

8. CONTENT SOURCE - where the never-ending supply of episodes comes from, so
   the channel doesn't run dry at video 30.

9. PRODUCTION REALITY - can this be made faceless with my time and budget?
   What's the hardest part of producing it?

10. FIRST 5 VIDEO TITLES - actual titles, ready to use.

Then rank all 8 from best to worst fit for MY specific situation and explain
the ranking in 2-3 sentences each.

Finally: tell me which ONE you'd pick and why, and flag any niche on the list
you think is a trap despite looking attractive.

PROMPT 2 - Channel Setup, Naming & Positioning
Act as a brand strategist for YouTube channels. I'm launching a faceless
channel in this niche: [NICHE FROM PROMPT 1].

Build me the complete channel identity:

1. CHANNEL NAMES - 15 options across 3 styles:
   - Direct/descriptive (says exactly what it is)
   - Evocative/curious (creates intrigue)
   - Authority (sounds established and credible)
   For each, note whether the .com is likely available and whether it's easy
   to say out loud and spell. Flag any that could be confused with an
   existing channel.

2. THE POSITIONING STATEMENT - one sentence: "This channel is for [specific
   person] who wants [specific outcome] without [specific frustration]."

3. CHANNEL DESCRIPTION - 3 versions (short for the banner, medium for the
   About section, long for SEO). Each must be readable by a human, not
   keyword soup.

4. VISUAL IDENTITY BRIEF - color palette with hex codes and the psychological
   reason for each choice, font pairing recommendation, thumbnail style rules
   (what stays consistent across every video so viewers recognize me in the
   feed).

5. THE CONTENT PILLARS - 4-5 recurring content categories this channel will
   rotate between, each with a one-line description and 3 example video
   topics. This is what stops the channel from becoming random.

6. THE PROMISE - what a viewer gets from every single video, stated in one
   sentence. This is the thing that must never be violated.

7. FIRST 10 VIDEOS IN LAUNCH ORDER - with reasoning for the sequence. Which
   one goes first and why? Which one is most likely to be the breakout?

8. WHAT THIS CHANNEL WILL NEVER DO - 5 specific things (formats, topics,
   tactics) that are off-brand. Constraints create identity.

PROMPT 3 - Video Ideation Engine

Generate 20 video ideas for my channel using the context above.

Rules before you start:
- No idea may be one that 100 other channels have already made this month
  unless the angle is genuinely new.
- Every idea needs at least one specific, concrete, researchable hook detail.
- Mix formats: don't give me 20 listicles.

For EACH idea:

1. TITLE - the actual title I'd publish, under 60 characters where possible.

2. THE HOOK - the exact first two sentences of the video, word for word.
   These must create an unfinished thought the brain can't drop.

3. THE CURIOSITY GAP - what specific question the video raises early and
   doesn't answer until later. Name the exact moment it pays off.

4. WHY SOMEONE CLICKS - the psychological driver in one line. Name it:
   curiosity / fear of missing something / vindication / disbelief /
   practical value / identity.

5. WHY SOMEONE STAYS PAST 2 MINUTES - what happens in the second minute that
   re-hooks them. This is where most faceless videos die.

6. THE COMMENT DRIVER - the specific element that makes people reply. Not
   "ask a question at the end" - what's built into the content that provokes
   a reaction.

7. THE SHARE DRIVER - why sharing this makes the sharer look good.

8. RESEARCH KEYWORDS - exactly what to look up to make this accurate. Mark
   anything I must verify with [VERIFY].

9. SERIES POTENTIAL - how this becomes episode 1 of a recurring format.

10. ESTIMATED DIFFICULTY - easy / medium / hard to produce, and why.

After the 20, rank the top 5 by breakout potential and explain what makes
each one stronger than the rest.
PROMPT 4 - Title Generator (the highest-leverage prompt here)
My video is about: [TOPIC]
The single most interesting fact in it is: [FACT]
My target viewer is: [PERSON]

Generate 20 title options. Do not describe the video make not clicking feel
like a mistake.

Organize them into these categories, 4 titles each:

CURIOSITY GAP states that something exists without saying what
Example structure: "The [thing] that [surprising outcome]  and nobody noticed"

CONTRADICTION - challenges something the viewer believes
Example structure: "[Common belief] is wrong. Here's what actually [happens]"

SPECIFICITY -uses a precise number, name, or detail that feels like insider info
Example structure: "The [exact number] [thing] that [outcome]"

STAKES - makes the consequence of not knowing feel real
Example structure: "What happens to [group] who [action] \ and why it matters now"

IDENTITY - makes the right viewer feel personally addressed
Example structure: "If you [specific situation], this is the [thing] nobody told you"

For each title, add:
- The psychological trigger in 3 words
- A predicted CTR tier (high / medium / low) with a one-line reason
- Character count

Then:
- Pick the single strongest title and explain in 3 sentences why it beats the
  other 19.
- Give me the 3 titles I should A/B test against it.
- Flag any title that overpromises something the video can't deliver I'd
  rather lose the click than burn trust.
PROMPT 5 - The Master Script Prompt (retention-engineered)
Write a full faceless YouTube script.

TOPIC: [TOPIC]
TARGET LENGTH: [X] minutes (approximately [X × 150] words of narration)
FORMAT: [documentary / explainer / story / listicle]
AUDIENCE: [SPECIFIC PERSON]

Your only job is to make it physically difficult to stop watching. Not
informative. Not educational-sounding. Addictive. Write it the way someone
tells an insane true story to a friend at 1am, not the way someone teaches
a class.

THE HOOK (first 15-20 seconds)
Open mid-story, never at the chronological beginning. Drop the viewer into
the most intense or confusing moment first, then pull back to explain how we
got there. The first sentence must create an unfinished story the brain can't
let go of. Do NOT explain what the video is about. Do NOT say "in this video."
Do NOT introduce the channel.

OPEN LOOPS EVERY 20-40 SECONDS
Never let information land without immediately raising a new question. The
moment you answer something, plant the next mystery in the same breath. If the
viewer could pause and accurately guess what comes next, you've failed.

PACING
Every sentence must move the story forward. If a sentence could be deleted
without losing information, tension, or emotion delete it. Short sentences
hit harder. Use fragments. Vary the rhythm constantly: three short punches,
then one longer sentence that lets the tension breathe, then back to short.

PATTERN INTERRUPTS EVERY 20-30 SECONDS
The video must never feel the same for more than 30 seconds. Interrupt with:
a one-line reveal, a direct question to the viewer, a tone shift, a "but
here's the part nobody talks about," a flash-forward tease, a contradiction
of what was just said.

CURIOSITY BEFORE INFORMATION
Never fully explain something the moment it's introduced. Mention that
something happened before explaining what or why. The gap between "something
happened" and "here's what happened" is where retention lives.

ESCALATION
Every section must raise the stakes above the one before it. The story cannot
plateau. Things must get worse, weirder, bigger, or more surprising as it
progresses.

EMOTION EVERY 30 SECONDS
Hit an emotional note constantly: fear, anger, awe, sympathy, vindication,
dread, surprise. After every section, ask: what is the viewer feeling right
now? If the answer is "nothing," rewrite it.

STORYTELLING, NOT EXPLAINING
Never say "this happened because of X." Put the viewer inside the moment and
let the cause reveal itself through what happens next. Show people doing and
saying things. A script that explains sounds like a textbook.

MICRO-REWARDS EVERY 20-30 SECONDS
Give the viewer something satisfying a small reveal, a confirmation of a
suspicion, an answer to a tiny earlier question, a detail that clicks
something into place.

SPECIFICITY
Real names, exact numbers, precise moments, exact words people said. Vague
generality is what makes a script feel fake.

MAKE THE VIEWER FEEL SMART
Structure reveals so the viewer almost gets there themselves a half-second
before you say it.

MINI-CLIFFHANGERS
End every section on a question, a contradiction, or a deliberately
incomplete statement. Never on a settled thought.

THE ENDING
Do not summarize. Do not say "and that's the story of." End on the single
most powerful image or realization in the piece something that recontextualizes
what came before. The last line should feel like a gut punch, not a conclusion.

HARD RULES:
- Never answer a question without raising a new one
- Never repeat a point in different words
- Never use "and" where "but" creates more tension
- Never use AI clichés ("little did they know," "everything changed forever")
- Never invent facts, quotes, or events mark uncertain claims [VERIFY]
- Never write a paragraph that wouldn't make a friend say "wait, what?"

FORMAT:
No section labels or structural markers. One continuous flowing piece. Include
one natural subscribe mention roughly halfway that doesn't break momentum.
End with a CTA that flows out of the final emotional beat.

Before finalizing, reread every paragraph and apply the "wait, what?" test.
Rewrite or cut anything that fails it.

PROMPT 6 Thumbnail Concept Generator
My video title is: [TITLE]
The core emotion of the video is: [EMOTION]
My channel's consistent visual style is: [DESCRIBE]

Generate 8 thumbnail concepts. The rule for all of them: one visual, one
emotion, one focal point. If it takes more than 3 seconds to understand at
postage-stamp size on a phone in bright sunlight, it fails.

For EACH concept:

1. THE CORE VISUAL = describe exactly what's in frame. Be specific enough
   that I could recreate or generate it without guessing.

2. THE TEXT = maximum 4 words. State the exact words. If the concept works
   with zero text, say so that's often stronger.

3. THE EMOTIONAL TRIGGER = what the viewer feels in the half-second before
   they read the title.

4. COLOR DIRECTION = with hex codes, and how it contrasts against a typical
   YouTube feed (which is mostly white/light grey).

5. THE CURIOSITY MECHANIC = what the image implies but doesn't resolve.
   A good thumbnail asks a question the title partially answers.

6. WHY IT WORKS AT SMALL SIZE = what's still legible when it's 3cm wide.

7. PRODUCTION NOTES = can this be made with stock footage, AI generation,
   or simple graphics? What's the fastest route to making it?

Then:
- Rank all 8 by predicted click-through rate with reasoning.
- Identify which 2 I should A/B test against each other and why.
- Flag any concept that clashes with my established channel style consistency
  in the feed matters more than any single thumbnail winning.

PROMPT 7 - SEO, Description & Metadata
My video: [TITLE]
Topic: [TOPIC]
Target keyword: [KEYWORD]

Produce the complete metadata package:

1. DESCRIPTION = three parts:
   - First 2 lines (the only part visible before "show more"): must hook and
     contain the primary keyword naturally
   - Body: 150-250 words summarizing the video's value, written for a human,
     using the keyword and 3-5 related terms naturally. No keyword stuffing.
   - Footer: placeholder slots for links, affiliate disclosure, and social

2. TAGS = 15 tags in priority order: exact-match keyword, close variants,
   broader category terms, and 2-3 competitor-channel-adjacent terms.

3. CHAPTERS = 6-10 timestamped chapters. Each chapter title should be written
   as a search phrase someone would actually type, because chapters rank
   independently in search. Never use "Intro / Part 1 / Part 2."

4. PINNED COMMENT = written to provoke replies, not to summarize the video.
   It should ask something specific that people have an opinion about.

5. THE DUAL-PURPOSE TITLE CHECK = is my title written for YouTube search or
   Google search? Give me one alternate title optimized for the other, since
   some topics rank in Google SERPs as video results.

6. END SCREEN STRATEGY = which 2 of my existing videos should I link, and
   what's the logic (same-topic depth vs. adjacent curiosity)?

7. COMMUNITY POST = a short post to publish 24 hours after upload that drives
   returning viewers back to this video without feeling like spam.

PROMPT 8 = The Retention Diagnosis
Act as a retention analyst. Here's my data:

VIDEO: [TITLE]
Views: [X] | Impressions: [X] | CTR: [X]% | Average view duration: [X]% |
Subs gained: [X]

RETENTION GRAPH DESCRIPTION: [describe the shape where the drops are, how
steep, whether it recovers. Include timestamps of the biggest drops.]

TRANSCRIPT OR SCRIPT: [paste it]

Diagnose this video:

1. THE PRIMARY LEAK - where is the single biggest loss happening, and is it
   a packaging problem (CTR), an opening problem (0-30s), a pacing problem
   (steady decline), or a payoff problem (drop right before the end)?

2. THE EXACT SENTENCES THAT COST ME VIEWERS quote the specific lines in my
   script that correspond to the biggest drop points and explain what went
   wrong at each one.

3. THE 0-30 SECOND AUDIT = line by line, does my opening create an unfinished
   thought? Where exactly does it stop being compelling?

4. THE MIDDLE-SECTION AUDIT = find every stretch longer than 40 seconds
   without a new question, reveal, or pattern interrupt. List them with
   timestamps.

5. THE REWRITE = rewrite my three worst-performing sections completely, using
   the retention principles. Show the before and after side by side.

6. WHAT I DID RIGHT = identify the sections with the strongest retention and
   explain the mechanism, so I can deliberately repeat it.

7. THE ONE CHANGE = if I could only fix one thing before my next upload, what
   is it and why?

Be blunt. I want the real diagnosis, not encouragement.

PROMPT 9 - Repurposing Engine
Here is my full video script: [PASTE SCRIPT]

Break this single asset into a month of content across platforms. For each
piece, give me the actual finished copy not a description of what to make.

1. SHORTS / TIKTOKS = 5 clips. For each: the exact timestamp range to cut,
   the standalone hook line to add at the front (since it needs to work with
   zero context), and the text overlay. Each clip must make sense to someone
   who's never seen the full video.

2. X THREAD = one thread of 8-10 posts covering the video's core argument.
   The first post must work as a standalone tweet. Written in lowercase,
   conversational, no corporate phrasing.

3. STANDALONE TWEETS = 6 tweets pulled from the strongest single lines or
   reframes in the script. Each must land without any context.

4. INSTAGRAM CAROUSEL = 8 slides. Give me the exact text for each slide and
   a one-line description of the visual.

5. COMMUNITY POST = a question that gets replies and pulls people back to
   the video.

6. EMAIL / NEWSLETTER VERSION = 300 words, written as if I'm telling one
   person about this over coffee.

7. THE NEXT VIDEO = based on what's in this script, what's the single most
   obvious follow-up video my audience will want? Give me the title and hook.

Rules: no piece may just be a truncated version of another. Each one has to
work on its own terms for its own platform.

PROMPT 10 - Monetization & Offer Strategy
My channel: [NICHE], [X subscribers], averaging [X views/video].
My audience: [DESCRIBE THEM SPECIFICALLY]

Build my complete monetization roadmap:

1. REVENUE LAYERS IN ACTIVATION ORDER = for each layer tell me: what it is,
   when to turn it on (what threshold), realistic monthly revenue at my
   current size, and the single biggest mistake people make with it.
   Cover: affiliates, email capture, digital products, ad revenue, sponsorships,
   and one path most channels in my niche ignore.

2. AFFILIATE PROGRAMS = 8 specific programs relevant to MY audience, with
   typical commission structure, and a one-line note on why my viewers would
   actually buy it. Mark any you're not certain still exist with [VERIFY].
   Prioritize programs where the product genuinely helps my viewer a bad
   recommendation costs more trust than 50 good videos earn.

3. THE LEAD MAGNET - one specific free resource I could make in under 3 hours
   that my audience would genuinely want. Give me its title, its contents in
   outline form, and the exact one-line pitch to use in video descriptions.

4. THE FIRST DIGITAL PRODUCT = what to sell, at what price, and why that
   price. Include the full outline and the specific problem it solves that
   the free content doesn't.

5. NATURAL INTEGRATION SCRIPTS = write 3 different ways to mention an offer
   inside a video that don't break the viewing experience. They must sound
   like a person recommending something, not an ad read.

6. THE TRUST RULES = 5 specific rules I should never break when monetizing
   this audience, based on what would make them feel sold to rather than
   served.

7. 12-MONTH PROJECTION = realistic (not optimistic) revenue by month, showing
   which layer contributes what. Be honest about how slow the first 4 months
   are.

The order to run these
Week 0 (setup): Prompt 0 = Prompt 1 = Prompt 2 Every week after: Prompt 0 = Prompt 3 (ideas) = Prompt 4 (title) = Prompt 5 (script) = Prompt 6 (thumbnail) = Prompt 7 (metadata) Every 2 weeks: Prompt 8 on your worst-performing video After each upload: Prompt 9 Once at month 2, then quarterly: Prompt 10
Three rules that protect the output quality

Never run two prompts in one session. Depth collapses the moment you stack requests. One prompt, one session, full attention.

Feed your real performance data back in. After 3-4 uploads, add to Prompt 0: "Videos like [your best performer] are working. Videos like [your worst] are not. Weight accordingly." This is how the pack gets smarter than any generic prompt.

Verify every fact before publishing. The [VERIFY] flags exist for a reason. One fabricated statistic in a video costs more credibility than ten good videos earn back.

Statement : The blocking of BitChat's code on GitHub is unconstitutional and authoritarian. 

New Delhi, 24 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the order issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, directing GitHub to remove the code repositories of BitChat. 

The order, Notice No. 11072601011432, was issued at 11:16 pm on 23 July 2026 under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021. The order directs GitHub to disable access to three repositories, including the Android application and its release files, within three hours. It threatens the platform with loss of safe harbour and criminal prosecution. No copy was published by the Government of India. The public learnt of it from a post by @jack, whose team develops BitChat. Censorship in India now comes to light through disclosure by the censored.

Since 17 July 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs has suspended mobile internet around Jantar Mantar as per public reports about five times, most recently within a 1.5 kilometre radius from 4 pm until midnight on 23 July. That radius takes in Janpath and parts of Connaught Place. Reports describe signal jammers at the protest site and people walking two kilometres before their phones work. Inside that zone a student separated from her group during a detention drive cannot send a message to say where she is. Thousands of students and young people have camped at Jantar Mantar since June, seeking accountability for examination irregularities. Permission for their march to Parliament was refused. Metro stations were shut and also internet connectivity has been blocked.

BitChat is an open source application built for exactly this situation. It passes messages from phone to phone over Bluetooth, without mobile networks or a central server. It is striking that the order does not identify a single unlawful message. It objects to what BitChat is. In its own words, the application is dangerous because it enables communication "even during network restrictions" and can "circumvent lawful restrictions" during "internet shutdowns". Hence, the government's objection is that citizens can speak to one another while it has switched the internet off. 

The order is illegal on at least four grounds. 

1. Section 79(3)(b) is not a blocking power. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down the provision. Intermediaries may be required to act only on a court order, or a government notification confined to the grounds under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Blocking is governed exclusively by Section 69A and the Blocking Rules, 2009, which require a hearing and reasons recorded in writing, subject to review. Directions issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal evade these safeguards, and constitutional challenges to this parallel regime are pending before High Courts. 

2. The reasons in the order are circular. The order asserts that the repositories contain "information which is prohibited under any law" without naming any such information, and rests on what the application is "capable of" enabling. Anticipated misuse of a communications tool is not a lawful basis to prohibit the tool. By this logic a telephone exchange could be sealed. 

3. The order cites Section 43 of the IT Act, a civil compensation provision, alongside conspiracy and abetment offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, against a platform that hosts code. 

4. A three hour deadline issued close to midnight forecloses legal assessment and recourse, and fails the proportionality standard in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637.

The order also fails on its own terms as deleting a repository does not delete the application from any phone that carries it, and the mesh keeps functioning without servers. What the takedown actually prevents is scrutiny of the underlying code.

IFF demands that the Government of India:

1. Withdraw Notice No. 11072601011432 dated 23 July 2026 issued to GitHub.
2. Publish every takedown direction issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal, with the reasons recorded for each.
3. Restore full connectivity around Jantar Mantar, publish all suspension orders, and disclose the legal authority for the deployment of jammers.

We stand with the developers and the young protesters whose speech this order seeks to silence.

Balochistan High Court Issues Notices on BYC Petition Challenging Faceless Trials

Baloch Yakjehti Committee

The Baloch Yakjehti Committee (BYC) welcomes the proceedings of the Balochistan High Court on the constitutional petition filed against the conduct of faceless trials and the restrictions imposed on open and public court proceedings.

On 11 August 2026, the Balochistan High Court issued notices to the respondents on the petition filed by Dr. Mahrang Baloch, Beebow Baloch, Gul Zadi Baloch, Sibghatullah Shah Ji and Bebarg Baloch, who are currently facing trial while in custody at District Jail Quetta. The petition challenges the relevant government notifications issued on 24 November 2025, 10 October 2025 and 12 June 2026, as well as the application of Section 21 of the Anti-Terrorism Act.

The petition seeks to declare these notifications unlawful, unconstitutional, and violative of Articles 4, 9, 10-A, 14, 25, and 175(3) of the Constitution of Pakistan. In addition to challenging the notifications, the petition formally prays the Honorable Court to declare that any trial conducted under the shadow of executive threats and in the secrecy of a prison environment, as well as any proceedings held in the absence of the petitioners and their defense counsel, are null and void. Furthermore, it requests the transfer of all cases and proceedings presently pending against the petitioners to another competent Court of law.

The petition also asks the Court to restrain the respondents from intervening, influencing, or exerting administrative or executive pressure on the pending proceedings or presiding officers. It seeks to restrain the state from appointing substitute or State-nominated counsel, ensuring the petitioners' right to counsel of their own choice is not defeated due to clashing hearing dates. Additionally, the petition asks the Court to direct authorities to grant the petitioners free, confidential, and unmonitored access to consult with their defense counsel for effective preparation of their defense, and to direct the respondents to restore and conduct all proceedings and hearings in a publicly accessible, open court prior to the issuance of the June 12 notification, in the larger interest of justice, equity, and fair play.

The issuance of notices by the High Court is an important step in bringing the legality and constitutionality of these measures before the Court for judicial consideration. The respondents will now be required to respond to the petition and explain the legal basis for the measures being challenged.

The BYC has consistently maintained that the right to a fair and transparent trial cannot be compromised through procedures that prevent public access to judicial proceedings. Court proceedings involving political and other detainees must remain subject to transparency, due process, and the protection of fundamental rights.

The use of closed or faceless proceedings raises serious concerns regarding transparency, accountability, and the right of an accused person to effectively defend themselves. Justice must not only be delivered according to law but must also be conducted through a process that remains open to public scrutiny.

The Baloch Yakjehti Committee considers this petition not merely a legal matter concerning its detained leadership, but an important question concerning the independence of the judiciary, transparency of judicial proceedings, due process, fundamental rights, and the rule of law.

BYC will continue to pursue all legal and peaceful avenues for the protection of the fundamental rights of its detained leaders and activists and will continue to demand transparent, open, and fair judicial proceedings.

Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. 🤔On August 12, 2026, the President of the United States signed a document that created something that didn't exist the day before.

The National Security Presidential Memorandum is titled "Expanding Capabilities to Combat Transnational Cyber-Enabled Crime." What it actually does is authorize vetted American private companies to conduct offensive cyber operations break-ins, disruption, sabotage against foreign criminal networks, under direct federal government oversight.

Read that again. Private companies. Offensive operations. Against foreign targets. Authorized by the President.

For the first time in American history, the federal government has formally deputized the private sector to attack.

Here's some history.

Article I, Section 8 of the United States Constitution grants Congress the power to "grant Letters of Marque and Reprisal." In the age of sail, a letter of marque was a government license authorizing a private ship to attack enemy vessels. The private captain operated under his own flag, with his own crew, at his own risk but with the legal authority of the sovereign behind him. He wasn't a pirate. He was a privateer. The difference was the piece of paper.

Letters of marque were how small nations punched above their weight at sea. You didn't need a massive navy if you could authorize your merchant fleet to fight. The private sector was faster, more innovative, and more numerous than any government fleet. All it needed was permission.

The United States just issued the digital equivalent.

The NSPM creates two categories of authorized private action.

The first is Cyber Surveillance Operations — gathering intelligence on foreign criminal networks, mapping their infrastructure, identifying their operators.

The second is Cyber Effects Operations. "Effects" is the government's word for disruption, degradation, and sabotage. Breaking things. Shutting systems down. Making the enemy's tools stop working.

Both categories are conducted under the direction, control, and authority of the federal government. The private companies don't freelance. They propose operations to the National Coordination Center, which sits under the Homeland Security Task Force and is run by two Executive Directors from the Department of Justice and the Department of Homeland Security. The operations are reviewed, approved, and overseen by federal authorities. The Homeland Security Council establishes the procedures.

The private company provides the capability. The government provides the authority. Together they do what neither could do alone.

The predicate is a number: $20.8 billion.

That's how much Americans lost to cyber-enabled crime in 2025. Twenty billion dollars stolen by foreign criminal organizations operating from jurisdictions where American law enforcement has no reach. Countries that don't cooperate with extradition. Countries that don't investigate cybercrime. Countries that might be quietly benefiting from it.

The traditional options were diplomacy, sanctions, and whatever the intelligence community could do in classified programs nobody talks about. The NSPM adds a fourth option: unleash the American private sector.

The memorandum states it plainly. "The American private sector is the most innovative and technologically advanced in the world, and its scale, speed, and capacity secure a critical offensive cyber advantage for the United States." And then: "American businesses' innovative capabilities have historically been underutilized in efforts to identify and disrupt criminal networks operating in cyberspace."

Underutilized. Past tense. That era ended on August 12.

This didn't come out of nowhere. There's a sequence.

On March 6, 2026, the President signed Executive Order 14390 "Combating Cybercrime, Fraud, and Predatory Schemes Against American Citizens." That order directed federal agencies to develop action plans. It created the NCC's operational cell framework. But it stopped short of the critical step: authorizing private companies to act.

Five months later, the NSPM provides that authorization. EO 14390 was the blueprint. The NSPM is the building permit.

And two days before the NSPM was signed, a private crypto exchange called Bybit sued North Korea's Lazarus Group in U.S. federal court and won a preliminary injunction freezing $1.5 billion in stolen assets. A private company, using the American legal system, against a sovereign state's hacking apparatus. The civil version of what the NSPM now authorizes in the operational domain.

Here's what this means for everything else that's been happening.

Treasury designates crypto exchanges used by Iran's Revolutionary Guard and publishes their wallet addresses. OFAC sanctions shadow banking networks. FinCEN assesses $125 million penalties against banks that fail to catch illicit flows. The Enforcement Directorate in India seizes $2.4 billion from a single conglomerate. China sentences defense ministers to death. Russia builds surveillance architecture over its own crypto markets. Nineteen nations form a military coalition in Panama.

All of those are governments acting through government instruments. Sanctions, seizures, indictments, designations, military coalitions.

The NSPM says: that's not enough. The government will also authorize private companies to conduct offensive cyber operations against the same criminal networks that everyone else is trying to dismantle through traditional enforcement.

The government built the enforcement architecture. Now it's handing some of the tools to the private sector and saying: help us use them. You're faster. You're more innovative. You're already in the networks. Here's your letter of marque. Go hunting.

I am the guy on the couch, and you have been debriefed.

🤔Three days ago, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said: "Whether in dollars, rials, or crypto, Treasury will hunt down and dismantle the illicit financial networks."

Today, Russia legalized cryptocurrency trading under Central Bank supervision.

The natural reading is that Russia is building an escape route. The U.S. keeps shutting down Russian crypto exchanges Garantex in 2025, Grinex's wallets frozen by Tether so Russia built its own regulated market that operates under Russian law, beyond the reach of American sanctions enforcement.

That reading is wrong.

Read the law.

Here's what Russia actually built.

State-registered exchanges. Only organizations entered in a government register can operate. Digital depositories that maintain records of ownership. Investor testing requirements before anyone can trade. Annual caps non-qualified investors can purchase no more than 300,000 rubles, about $4,000, per year per broker. Central Bank oversight of every exchange, custodian, and intermediary.

Every transaction recorded. Every owner known. Every exchange supervised.

Before this law, Russian crypto activity ran through Garantex, Grinex, shadow OTC desks, and Telegram brokers. Those channels were dark. Not just dark to the U.S. Treasury. Dark to Russia. Russian intelligence didn't know what was moving through Russian crypto infrastructure any better than Washington did.

Now they will.

And then there's the line in the law that tells you everything.

Cryptocurrencies are approved for cross-border settlements. They are banned as domestic payment methods.

You can use crypto to move value across borders. You cannot use it to buy anything inside Russia. The law separates the two uses and legalizes only the one that Russia's government wants to monitor international flows.

So what did Russia actually do?

It didn't build an escape route from transparency. It built a surveillance architecture for its own crypto flows. It took the activity that was running through shadows and told it: come inside where we can see you, or you're a criminal under Russian law too.

Think about what this means for the person operating in the dark.

Before the law, a Russian businessman moving money through a Telegram OTC desk was in a gray area. There was no law regulating it, so there was no law to break. He was invisible to Moscow and invisible to Washington.

After the law, that same businessman has a choice. Move onto the registered exchange where the Central Bank sees every transaction, the digital depository records his ownership, and his annual volume is capped and monitored. Or stay in the shadows where he is now breaking Russian law, not just American sanctions.

Before, he was hiding from one government. Now he's hiding from two.

Both sovereigns are squeezing from both sides. The operator who stays in the dark is a criminal in Moscow and in Washington. Not because they coordinated. Because they both built the same thing for their own reasons.

This is what every country covered in this series has been doing.

The United States built the GENIUS Act framework, requiring stablecoin issuers to implement bank-grade know-your-customer rules. Treasury designated crypto exchanges laundering money for Iran and published on-chain wallet addresses so that every participant in the system can screen for sanctioned flows.

India formally designated its Enforcement Directorate as the lead agency for seized cryptocurrency. Its Criminal Investigation Department, with Binance's help, busted a crypto-hawala network linked to Hamas and Houthi organizations.

China is running the largest anti-corruption purge in its history six sectors of its own government, two former defense ministers sentenced to death, the former head of China Development Bank under investigation.

Saudi Arabia's anti-corruption body Nazaha arrests over a hundred officials every month.

Mexico's current Attorney General arrested the former Attorney General. Then she arrested a former governor.

Colombia's new president captured a narcotrafficking commander 48 hours after inauguration.

Syria's first judicial act as a new government was sentencing its former president to death for using the state as a weapon.

And now Russia the country under the most comprehensive sanctions regime in history has built a regulated, supervised, recorded crypto market under its own Central Bank. Not to evade transparency. To impose it. On its own people. For its own purposes.

Every government in the world is doing the same thing.

They are forcing activity out of the dark and onto infrastructure they control. They are building transparent rails. They are telling the people who operate in the shadows: come where we can see you, or you are a criminal. Not because anyone told them to. Because every sovereign has the same interest in knowing where the money is.

The United States wants to see the flows so it can enforce sanctions. Russia wants to see the flows so it can control capital flight and fund its war. China wants to see the flows so it can purge corruption. India wants to see the flows so it can prosecute money laundering. Saudi Arabia wants to see the flows so it can break the old patronage networks.

Different reasons. Same architecture. Same outcome.

The money has nowhere left to hide not because one government closed all the doors, but because every government is closing its own doors, from the inside, for its own reasons.

That's not coordination.
That's convergence.

Bartz v. Anthropic settled at $1.5 billion for 500,000 pirated works. Zero analysts in the acquiring firm's data room had flagged training data provenance as a risk before close.

An acquirer I work with inherited that same category of problem six months after signing. The target company had scraped public medical journals to build its classification model, and two publishers sent cease-and-desist letters within weeks of the acquisition announcement. 

The publishers identified 200 journal articles in the training dataset, with licensing fees running $4,000 per article per year of use. The company had trained on those articles for three years. The acquirer's legal team spent four months and $800K negotiating a retroactive bulk license, and the cost came from the integration budget because the deal model hadn't priced it.

The acquirer's CTO told me she had reviewed the company's data architecture during diligence. She examined database schemas and API integrations, but she did not examine the provenance of the training datasets because her diligence checklist, built for traditional SaaS, didn't include that line item. 

A publisher's lawyer raised the training data question eight weeks after close. The CTO hadn't covered it in her review.

You acquire an AI company and you acquire the data sourcing decisions its engineers made over years. 

Those decisions live in scraping logs and data pipeline configurations that diligence teams don't open. 

The IP section of the data room covers patents and trademarks, but most teams leave training data provenance out of their review because the standard checklist doesn't account for it.

The EU AI Act is live. Fines run up to 35 million euros or 7% of global turnover for non-compliance with data governance requirements for high-risk AI systems. The regulation mandates documented training data sources and conformity assessments. 

If your portfolio company trained its model on data it doesn't have the right to use, the liability transfers to you at close, and EU regulators can enforce against the current owner.

Operating partners can tell you what software the company licenses, but fewer of them can tell you where the training data originated or whether the team holds documented rights to use it.

A training data audit runs on two dimensions. 

First, lineage: I check whether the engineering team can trace each training dataset back to its source, with collection dates and licensing terms. Most teams I assess cannot produce this documentation within the two-week assessment window because the engineers who built the model didn't record their data sources at the time. 

Second, the synthetic data ratio: I measure the percentage of training data the team generated versus the percentage collected from external sources. Synthetic data carries lower legal exposure, and a company with a high synthetic ratio has lower tail risk on IP claims.

I find the same thing at each target: engineering teams build models fast and treat data sourcing documentation as a problem for later. The acquiring company inherits the documentation gap along with the model.

The cease-and-desist letters arrive after close. The engineering team made those data sourcing decisions years before. 

You have the window between LOI and close to assess the risk, and most deal teams spend it on financial diligence instead.
