OK FINE, HERE IS A VERY DETALIED, ALL GAMES YOU CAN PLAY BEFORE KINGDOMHEARTS 4, this is good for people who are new to the series:

Kingdom Hearts Final Mix:
This is the foundation of everything. The original game introduces the core philosophy of the series. Hearts, connections, the power of friendship, the existence of other worlds, and the constant pull between light and darkness. It establishes the main trio and the fundamental rules of how this universe operates. Without it, every later game feels like it's referencing a language you never learned. Skipping this is like trying to understand a cathedral by only looking at the roof.

The Final Mix version isn't optional and here's why. The original 2002 release ends with a secret movie. Final Mix swaps it for a longer, weirder cut full of imagery that wouldn't pay off for eight more years. Eight years. People theorized about that video on forums for most of a decade. Final Mix also adds a hidden boss in Hollow Bastion who will make absolutely no sense to you, which is correct and intended, plus rebalanced difficulty and a bunch of extra content.

Now the important part. The Ansem Reports. There are thirteen of them, they're collectible text documents rather than cutscenes, and they contain a genuinely huge chunk of the game's real worldbuilding. The nature of the Heartless, what happened under Hollow Bastion, the question about identity that the entire second game is built on. Cutscene compilations on YouTube do not include them. Read them.

I'm going to keep bringing this up, because "Kingdom Hearts has an incoherent story" and "I watched the cutscene movies and skipped all the text documents" turn out to be the same sentence.
Play on Proud Mode always. Just because that's where the combat stops being a mash button simulator and starts making sense.

Kingdom Hearts Re: Chain of Memories
This is where the series starts showing you that memory itself is a battlefield. The card based combat forces you to think differently, but the real importance is how it expands the idea that identity and recollection are fragile. New players underestimate this one constantly because of the gameplay shift. Narratively it is load bearing.

Some background that makes it land better. The original Chain of Memories was a Game Boy Advance game from 2004, done in sprites, with a deck building system that is honestly way smarter than it had any right to be. You build a deck, you chain three cards together into special attacks called sleights, and enemies can break your card by playing a higher number. There's a card that breaks literally anything and is itself broken by literally anything. This is a real strategy game hiding inside a Disney licensed handheld title and people still don't take it seriously.

Re:Chain of Memories is the PS2 remake, originally released in Japan bundled with Kingdom Hearts II Final Mix Plus in 2007 and not localized until a standalone US release the following year. Full 3D, voice acting, card system mostly intact, which is a small miracle.

Do not skip Reverse Rebirth, the second campaign that unlocks after the main story. Different protagonist, completely different deck philosophy, no customization, and character material that Kingdom Hearts II opens by assuming you already have. If you've ever seen someone say "wait why is he like that at the start of KH2," you've met someone who skipped Reverse Rebirth.
Also the journal entries. More text. Still important. Read them.

Kingdom Hearts II Final Mix
This is widely considered the peak of the series for pure gameplay and spectacle, but its real value is how it deepens the themes of identity and belonging, and what happens when people are connected in ways they don't fully understand. It expands the cast massively and starts weaving a much bigger web of relationships and organizations. This is where the series stops being "Sora's adventure" and becomes a full ensemble story.

The Final Mix content is genuinely mandatory rather than just nice to have.
The Cavern of Remembrance is an entire post game area added in Final Mix, full of platforming, gauntlets, and a set of data battles that are basically the thesis statement of KH2's combat system. Every hard boss in every later Kingdom Hearts descends from these fights.
The Lingering Will is a Final Mix superboss and I'm not going to tell you a single thing about it. If you play KH2FM before Birth by Sleep, this fight is a screaming question mark. That's the intended experience and it rules.
The extended cutscenes throughout, including extra material in the Twilight Town prologue, which is substantially better than the original version.
The secret ending, unlocked by clearing the game and hitting the journal requirements. This one set up the next five years of the franchise.
Play on Critical Mode, which Final Mix introduced. Less HP and MP, but you start with bonus abilities and damage modifiers. It isn't a masochism setting, it's the difficulty the combat was actually tuned around, and it turns Reaction Commands and Drive Forms from spectacle buttons into an actual system you have to respect.
Final Mix also added the Zero EXP ability, which exists so people can do Level 1 Critical runs. You do not have to do this. But you should know it exists, because it's the closest thing this series has to a competitive scene and those runs are incredible to watch.

Kingdom Hearts 358/2 Days
Even if you only experience it as the HD cutscene movie, this is one of the best character studies in the entire franchise. It's about daily life, routine, friendship, and the quiet moments between the big events. It teaches you that the series cares just as much about the people living inside the conflict as it does about the conflict. A lot of later emotional beats only hit as hard as they do because this game spent time making you care.

The original is a Nintendo DS game from 2009 and it's a genuinely strange thing. The whole structure is a mission calendar. You get handed a day, a job, and a checklist, and the repetition is the entire point. The game is about routine. The HD version in Kingdom Hearts HD 1.5 ReMIX turns it into a three hour cutscene film, which keeps every story beat and completely wrecks the thesis. This is the most argued about adaptation decision in the series and you should absolutely have an opinion about it by the end.

What the movie loses, in case you can get the DS version running.

Mission Mode, with playable versions of all fourteen Organization members, each with their own weapon and moveset. It's the only place several of them are ever playable and it's fantastic.
The panel system, where your equipment, abilities, magic, and even your character level all live on one shared grid. Absolutely bizarre, weirdly great.
The secret reports, written from a perspective the cutscenes leave out, which supply motive and interiority the film version only implies. Yes. More text documents. This series really wants you to read.
Whatever you do, don't skip the entry. Watch the film and grab the reports separately if you have to.

Kingdom Hearts Birth by Sleep Final Mix:
The first major prequel and absolutely essential. New trio, new perspective, and stories that turn out to be tangled up with the main timeline in ways you won't see coming. The three route structure makes you live through the same events from different angles, which is a core Kingdom Hearts storytelling move you'll see again and again.
Play in Terra, then Ventus, then Aqua order. This is not fan preference, it's the intended reading order. The routes are written so each one gives you more information than the last, which means the dramatic irony compounds as you go. Playing Aqua first defuses the entire structure. Please don't.
This is a PSP game from 2010 and it's where the Command Deck comes from. No traditional MP bar, just a set of action slots on cooldown. Command Melding lets you fuse two commands plus a crystal into something new with abilities attached, and it has a real optimization ceiling. This system directly shapes Dream Drop Distance, Re:coded, and arguably KH3.

Final Mix specifics you can't skip.

The Secret Episode, unlocked after the Final Episode once you've collected all the reports. Short, and a direct bridge into a later entry.
The Xehanort Reports, thirteen of them, and the most important text collection in the series after the Ansem Reports. They lay out how the whole plan actually functions. I'll say this as plainly as I can. Almost every person I've ever seen call this plot incoherent has not read these.
The Mirage Arena, expanded in Final Mix, and the secret ending, which sets up the next game and recontextualizes something you already watched.
One nerd detail worth having. The χ blade shows up here, and that's the Greek letter chi, not the letter X. How you pronounce it eventually stops being a fandom argument and becomes an actual plot point, which is very funny and very on brand.

Kingdom Hearts Re:coded
Constantly dismissed as filler, and it's really not. This is where the series works out how it feels about data, digital worlds, and whether a reconstructed experience can carry real emotional truth. It connects earlier events to later ones in quiet ways and reinforces the idea that no story is ever really finished.

Fun historical footnote. The original coded was an episodic Japanese mobile phone game released between 2008 and 2010. On flip phones. In a delivery format that no longer exists in any playable form anywhere. Re:coded is the DS remake and it's the only version anyone outside Japan has ever legitimately played. The original is basically lost media.

Honest take, and your friends will respect you more for making it. Most of Re:coded's plot critical content is concentrated in the last stretch and the secret ending. The rest is a genuinely inventive gameplay experiment, with a stat grid, a bug block system, and worlds that change genre on you, wrapped around a story that's retreading familiar ground.

But the "data can hold real weight" idea isn't filler at all in hindsight. It's the philosophical groundwork for a much later arc. Re:coded is the series quietly setting its terms years in advance, and that's the kind of thing that makes people fall in love with this franchise.

Kingdom Hearts Dream Drop Distance
This is the game that formally kicks off the final stretch of the original arc while also planting seeds for everything after. It deepens the relationship between the main characters, expands the dream mythology, and introduces ideas later titles keep coming back to. This is where the scope starts feeling genuinely enormous.

3DS, 2012, and mechanically the most maximalist entry in the series. Flowmotion lets you grind rails and kick off walls and generally trivialize level geometry, and it was so much fun that later games quietly nerfed it out of existence. The Drop gauge is a timer that forcibly swaps you between the two protagonists mid dungeon, which is either brilliant thematic design or the most annoying system ever shipped, and you will have to pick a side. And the Dream Eater system replaces party members with craftable, raisable creature companions on an ability grid.

The ending sequence has the densest lore dump in the franchise up to that point. It also lays out a set of rules that are much stricter and more consistent than people give them credit for. Understanding those rules is genuinely the difference between "this is nonsense" and "oh, this is actually airtight." I will not be elaborating.

You'll play the HD version inside Kingdom Hearts HD 2.8 Final Chapter Prologue. Read the secret reports. I keep saying it. I will keep saying it.

Kingdom Hearts χ [chi]
The furthest back in the timeline and foundational for the whole new arc that Kingdom Hearts IV is entering. It introduces the ancient history of the Keyblade, the Foretellers, and the original conflict that still echoes into the present day. Without it, a big chunk of the mythology the series has been slowly revealing feels like it came out of nowhere.

Here's where the preservation situation gets grim. Kingdom Hearts χ was a Japan only Flash browser game launched in 2013, and the service was shut down in 2016. It's unplayable. You can't buy it. It exists now only as cutscene compilations put together by fans, and honestly the fan preservation community is the only reason this material is accessible at all. Genuinely, thank you to those people.

What you want out of it is the Age of Fairy Tales, the Book of Prophecies, the Master of Masters, and the five Foretellers, each with an animal masked Keyblade and each leading a Union. If you retain nothing else, retain those names and the fact that there's a black box nobody will tell you anything about. That box has been a running fandom obsession for over a decade.

Kingdom Hearts χ Back Cover
A short companion piece to χ focused on a specific group and their roles in the ancient conflict. Short, dense, and one of those small but load bearing things later games assume you already understand.

About an hour, fully animated in the KH3 engine, included in HD 2.8. It retells the events of χ from a different set of eyes, and it might be the single best directed piece of storytelling in the entire franchise. Which is a slightly funny thing to say about a bonus movie, but here we are.

Watch it after χ, not before. The perspective shift only works if you've got the ground level version first.

Kingdom Hearts Union χ [Cross]
The continuation and expansion of the χ storyline, and right now one of the most important things you can experience before Kingdom Hearts IV. It develops the ancient era further, deals with the fallout of the original conflict, and follows characters whose influence reaches all the way into the modern day. A lot of the threads the series is pulling on now start here.

The naming history is a disaster and you deserve to know it. This launched internationally in 2016 as Kingdom Hearts Unchained χ, a mobile remake and continuation of the dead browser game, then got rebranded to Union χ [Cross] in 2017 when the Union Cross multiplayer mode arrived. Same product, one continuous storyline, three names.

I'm going to break from the "everything is required" position for exactly one paragraph. This is sixty plus hours of cutscenes wrapped around a gacha, and a well edited summary is a completely legitimate way to consume it. A newcomer who watches ninety focused minutes is better prepared than one who bounces off the full archive at hour eleven. Nobody is grading you.

One thing you have to plan around. Union χ's live service has ended, and its ending was never part of the live game at all. It got delivered through a separate offline app alongside the finale of the next entry. Which brings me to the ordering fix.

Kingdom Hearts Dark Road
The last major piece of the ancient era puzzle. It follows the early life of a character whose importance becomes very clear very fast, and it fills in a lot of history about the Keyblade wielders and the world they lived in. It ties the distant past to the present in ways that matter directly for the new arc.

Move this up in your order. A lot of lists stick Dark Road at the very end, after Melody of Memory, and that's a release date artifact rather than a story order one. Dark Road's conclusion and Union χ's conclusion came out together and function as one sequence. Splitting them across a rhythm game in the middle is the one real ordering mistake I see people make. Watch or play Dark Road immediately after Union χ and it lands so much better.

Kingdom Hearts Missing Link ..... the game shaped hole
You can't play this one, and you should know why.

Missing Link was announced at the 20th Anniversary event in April 2022. GPS based mobile action RPG, Unreal Engine 5, gorgeous. Its story sat between Union χ and Dark Road, and it was explicitly meant to be connective tissue between Kingdom Hearts III and Kingdom Hearts IV. It went through multiple closed betas, got delayed in November 2024, and in May 2025 Square Enix cancelled it outright, saying they didn't think they could sustain a live service that would satisfy players long term.

So there's a gap in the chain that no amount of playing can fill. All that survives is beta footage, the official teasers, and a leaked opening cinematic. Whether that story content gets folded into KH4 or somewhere else hasn't been announced.

This isn't your fault and there's nothing to do about it. It's also, given the title, the funniest thing that has ever happened to this franchise.

Kingdom Hearts 0.2 Birth by Sleep, A Fragmentary Passage
Short but dense, and it sits right between the old saga and the new one. It follows one character through one very specific place, and it leans hard into isolation, determination, and the long term consequences of things that happened much earlier. It's placed exactly where it needs to be so that certain beats in Kingdom Hearts III land properly.

Two to three hours, part of HD 2.8, and functionally a tech demo for the KH3 engine. This is the first Kingdom Hearts content built in Unreal and you can feel every one of the eight years between it and the PSP original. It looks incredible.

It's also a genuinely useful mechanical warmup, since it's your first time with the KH3 command menu, Shotlocks, and situation commands. And yes, it has a secret ending, and yes, it matters.

Kingdom Hearts III plus Re Mind
The conclusion of the original long running story arc. Playing the base game is mandatory, and Re Mind is every bit as important. It expands the ending, adds significant new sequences, and introduces elements that set up the next era directly. Big payoff for everything before it, and the starting point for everything after.

What in Re Mind is genuinely not optional.

The Re Mind episode itself, which replays part of the endgame from a different angle with new scenes filling in gaps the base game very deliberately left open.

The Limit Cut episode, thirteen data fights, and much more importantly the cutscenes wrapped around them. There's more forward facing plot in those bookends than in the whole base game ending.

The Secret Episode, which is the most direct setup for Kingdom Hearts IV that currently exists. That's all I'm saying about it.

The base game's secret ending, which has its own unlock requirements involving photo missions and difficulty, so check them before you start rather than after.

One more thing to keep an eye on. There's a fake video game inside the Toy Box world. It plays like a Nomura self parody gag. It is not a gag. Pay attention to it and then come talk to me afterward, because watching people realize what that is in real time is one of my favorite things about this fandom.
And read the secret reports. Thirteen of them. Last time I'm saying it, I promise.

Kingdom Hearts Melody of Memory
This rhythm game is sneakily important. The gameplay is completely different, but the story sequences push the narrative past Kingdom Hearts III and set the emotional and thematic state of the cast heading into the new saga. It also works as a retrospective that helps everything you've played click into place.

Being straight with you, the story content is short. A framing narrative plus a substantial post credits sequence. That sequence is required. It's also about forty minutes of the runtime.

The other ninety five percent is a rhythm game with a setlist of well over a hundred and forty tracks pulled from Yoko Shimomura's entire body of work for the series. If you've just spent two hundred hours on everything above, playing the soundtrack in chronological order is one of the most quietly devastating retrospectives any franchise has ever built. Shimomura is one of the best composers this medium has, full stop, and Dearly Beloved gets rearranged for every entry in a way that tracks the emotional register of each game. Notice that while you play. It's the whole series in one melody.

Deep Cuts For Absolute Lunatics
Totally optional. You'll understand Kingdom Hearts IV without these. You will not be complete without them.

Kingdom Hearts V CAST from 2006, a Verizon exclusive mobile phone game released only in North America, retelling the first game in 2D with original world content. Delisted, never rereleased, effectively lost media, with fragments recovered by preservation people. Knowing this exists is a real flex in the right room.

Kingdom Hearts Mobile from 2008, Japan only, an avatar and social service with minigames. Not a story game. Listed purely because completeness demands it.

The Shiro Amano manga, covering the first game, Chain of Memories, KH2, 358/2 Days and more. Not canon, occasionally clarifying, frequently funnier than the games.

The Tomoco Kanemaki novels, light novel adaptations with interior monologue the games leave out. The 358/2 Days ones in particular contain characterization fans still quote.

The Ultimania guides, Japanese strategy guide and artbook hybrids stuffed with Nomura interviews that the fandom treats as basically canon because they keep answering things the games leave dangling. A surprising amount of well known Kingdom Hearts lore comes from an interview and has literally never been stated in a game.

The secret movies as their own thing. At some point, watch every secret ending in release order back to back as a standalone exercise. Twenty plus years of this series telegraphing itself. The through line is genuinely startling.

Actually Getting Your Hands On All This????
Kingdom Hearts Collection [I-III] comes out soon on October 8, 2026 on Switch 2, PS5, Xbox Series X and S, and PC. It bundles HD 1.5 plus 2.5 ReMIX, HD 2.8 Final Chapter Prologue, and KH3 with Re Mind, all running natively on current hardware. That one purchase covers twelve of the fourteen playable entries above, which is a genuinely great deal for a newcomer.

What it doesn't cover. Melody of Memory is a separate purchase. And the whole χ, Union χ, Dark Road line is dead mobile and browser stuff, so fan cutscene compilations are your only route.

You've got well over a year. Kingdom Hearts IV was confirmed at D23 in August 2026 for late 2027 all platforms basically 

Budget somewhere around 150 to 200 hours for the playable material at a normal pace, plus another 20 to 40 for the χ side of things depending on how completionist you get. Start now. Start with Final Mix. Play on Proud.

Everything on this list matters because Kingdom Hearts isn't a series of isolated stories. It's one continuous, self referential, multi decade narrative that treats every character, every world, every theme, and every mechanical idea as part of one living organism. It constantly rewards people who paid attention to the small details, the quiet character moments, the ancient history, and the questions it's been asking since 2002.

IFF's statement on the AI Impact Summit 2026.

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) welcomes the India AI Impact Summit 2026 (February 16-20) as an important platform for global dialogue on, "Artificial Intelligence". We believe the Summit's agenda and framing fundamentally misalign with the lived reality of AI deployment in India, an environment marked by rising digital authoritarianism and the systematic erosion of constitutional protections that are causing demonstrable harm to vulnerable populations. Its official framing centers on “People, Planet and Progress”, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurating and world leaders like France’s President Emmanuel Macron and top tech CEOs (Google’s Sundar Pichai, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, etc.) expected to attend. The Summit's optimistic narrative about AI for development obscures the reality of how its deployment is impacting people in their everyday lives.

The current environment is one of a sharp contraction in civic space, where recent governance proposals on technology have facilitated the expansion of state power that run contrary to the state commitments on fundamental rights and social justice. Today, there exists few organisations in India that work on digital rights and those which are surviving are severely under resourced, suffer from burdensome compliances, growing legal risks and deliberate exclusion from policy making processes. The decline of civil society work is matching the growth of private and public sector capacity to lobby the policy making processes. So, even before a question is prompted, how should Indian civil society engage with the India AI Impact Summit, a predicate and grounded inquiry is, how many independent, Indian civil society groups exist in India that have capacity and can be critical of state policies and practices around AI?

In the recent past, far from fostering accountability, India’s digitisation drive is often used to sidestep constitutional safeguards of transparency, harming communities and individuals. For instance, recent legal changes have weakened the Right to Information (RTI) framework, curtailing citizens’ ability to question power. The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023 introduced an amendment (Section 8(1)(j) to the RTI Act) that blocks access to any information labeled “personal information”, allowing officials to deny critical information. Likewise, digitisation of welfare governance has been weaponized to bypass accountability, with digitisation often becoming a gatekeeper and working to the detriment of the poor. A stark development came in December, 2025 when Parliament hastily passed the Viksit Bharat - Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025 (VB-GRAM G), repealing the landmark MGNREGA jobs guarantee program. VB-GRAM G converted a demand driven legal right to work into a discretionary, bureaucratically controlled scheme, undermining decades of workers’ rights. There are references to "AI" within the text of the objects and reasons that are a part of this law.

Beyond this, India's policies on AI also demonstrate a wider embrace of de-regulation narratives to ensure, "innovation". For instance, the Union Budget 2026 unveiled a 20-year tax holiday (until 2047) for foreign firms using Indian data centers, aiming to lure global AI infrastructure. Yet, this policy was formulated with scant regard for its impact on local communities and natural resources. Other recent measures also deserve comment:

Sanchar Saathi : In late 2025, the government ordered smartphone manufacturers to pre-install a government cybersecurity application called Sanchar Saathi on all devices. The app was ostensibly meant to secure citizens’ phones, but the mandatory installation sparked outrage over privacy and surveillance concerns, drawing parallels to spyware abuse.
The ‘Sahyog’ Censorship Portal: In 2024, the Union Home Ministry quietly launched the Sahyog Portal to expedite content-blocking orders on social media and websites. Under this system, law enforcement agencies can flag “unlawful” online content and directly trigger its takedown by internet platforms, all through a centralized interface.
Expansion of NATGRID: Perhaps the most far-reaching is the quiet expansion of NATGRID, India’s National Intelligence Grid. Long conceived as an integrated database for counter-terror investigations, NATGRID has recently morphed into a broad surveillance net. Following a high-level police conference in late November 2025, states were directed to “scale up” NATGRID usage beyond central agencies, even giving police officers at the Superintendent rank access to its vast datasets.
These developments match the increased use of AI technologies in domains of policing and welfare without a clear legal basis and real safeguards.

IFF acknowledges that the India AI Impact Summit 2026 offers a platform for dialogue and a chance for civil society voices to gain visibility on an international stage. We recognize the value in having digital rights perspectives included in global AI governance conversations, indeed, the Summit’s presence in India is an opportunity to spotlight our constitutional concerns before a world audience. We support our peer organizations and allies who choose to engage with the Summit, and we will remain in constructive collaboration with them. However, IFF has decided not to allocate significant organizational resources to direct participation in the Summit’s events. This is not a boycott of the forum, but a practical choice of focus. As a small team of only 7 full-time staff based in New Delhi, we must prioritize the most pressing advocacy initiatives that align closely with our mission and charter.

This includes ongoing efforts such as legal challenges to unconstitutional regulations, campaigning and community engagement for strengthening free expression, privacy and transparency frameworks. These are battles immediately affecting citizens’ rights and requiring our sustained attention. IFF will engage with the Summit in a mindful, critical manner. We will track the proceedings and outcomes closely, offering our analyses and critiques rooted in constitutional values. If and where we do participate (for example, in side events or discussions), we will do so with a critical gaze, centering the lived experiences of Indians and the paramountcy of our fundamental rights. Our support is firmly with the broader civil society coalition pushing for AI governance that is accountable and just.

A report by The Indian Express has highlighted the sharp rise in government-issued blocking orders to social media platforms between March and July, during the period of the CJP student protests.

Most of these directions were issued through the Sahyog portal, a government platform used by Central and state agencies to send blocking notices to social media companies. The report says many of these orders were issued under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, 2000, which requires intermediaries to remove unlawful content to retain their legal protection. Digital-rights advocates have raised concerns about this mechanism and its implications for due process and freedom of expression.

The Silent Emergency: Eleven Years Under the Shadow of Control

India, the land of a billion vibrant voices, is grappling with a chilling silence. For eleven years under the PM, we've witnessed an

"Undeclared Emergency@11"

—no declared curfews, no tanks, but a steady erosion of our democratic freedoms. This is the story of a Nation fighting for its soul, where the cost of speaking out grows heavier daily.

The Press in Chains
Our Fourth Estate, once a beacon of truth, now falters under relentless pressure. V-Dem and Freedom House 2025 reports label India an “electoral autocracy,” ranked “partly free.” The Press Freedom Index places us at 159/176, near Somalia’s shadow. Honest journalists face arrests, raids, and intimidation for daring to question. Laws like UAPA and sedition are weaponized, branding critics “terrorists” without trial. Media houses face raids, their voices stifled. Modi’s 11-year tenure without a single press conference speaks volumes—hate speech thrives, but truth is jailed.

Homes Turned to Rubble
Bulldozers roar across India, not for progress but as tools of vengeance. Homes, often of minorities or dissenters, are demolished in displays of state power. Families stand amid rubble, targeted for their identity or beliefs. Ministers spewing hate are rewarded, while citizens live in fear. This isn’t the India we fought for.

The Digital Gag
In the age of X, FB, Insta, and YouTube, where voices once soared, dissent is now caged. Content creators and tweeters face arrests for “misinformation” or “inciting unrest.” Over 20,000 independent voices have been silenced, their crime often a post challenging the regime. This is a democracy where keyboards are as dangerous as megaphones.

Opposition Under Siege
The Enforcement Directorate (ED) has become a weapon to intimidate opposition leaders, with raids targeting those who refuse to bow to the BJP. Homes and offices of opposition figures are stormed, cases piled up to coerce them into joining the ruling party or face relentless harassment. This blatant misuse of agencies undermines democracy, turning dissent into a dangerous act.

Puppet Election Commission
The Election Commission, once a pillar of democratic integrity, now dances to the tune of the BJP. The removal of the Chief Justice of India from the selection committee for appointing Election Commissioners has raised alarms about its independence. This move, critics argue, ensures a pliable EC, ready to tilt the electoral scales. Free and fair elections, the heartbeat of democracy, now pulse under the shadow of control.

The Leader’s Shadow
Modi’s image dominates—billboards, screens, even vaccine certificates and rail tickets. Supporters call it leadership; we see a cult stifling dissent. Parliament weakened, constitutional bodies eroded, divisive figures glorified—this is a five-fold assault on our democracy. BJP invokes 1975’s Emergency to deflect, but today’s control needs no formal name. It’s a slow, silent strangulation of our freedoms.

Nation’s Resolve
Fifty years ago, India resisted the 1975 Emergency. Today, the shackles are subtler but real. Jailed journalists, bulldozed homes, silenced voices, ED raids on opposition leaders, and a compromised Election Commission tell of a democracy under siege. As Modi marks “Samvidhan Hatya Diwas,” we say the real threat to our Constitution is now—unnamed, insidious, but ever-present.

India stands at a crossroads. Will we reclaim our chorus of voices or let silence prevail? The fight for our democracy lies in the courage of those who speak, write, and dream of a free tomorrow. 

#UndeclaredEmergency #SaveDemocracy

WHEN THE ELECTION WATCHDOG IS ASKED TO WATCH ITSELF

The Election Commission is supposed to be the referee of India’s elections. But what happens when citizens begin asking whether the referee is applying the rules equally?

Transparency activist Anjali Bhardwaj, in The Probe, raises precisely this uncomfortable question: are complaints of Model Code of Conduct violations being handled with the same urgency when they concern opposition leaders and leaders of the ruling party?

These are serious allegations—not facts that should be accepted merely because they are made in a video. But they deserve answers.

The 2019 election provides a telling historical example. NaMo TV, a channel devoted to Narendra Modi’s speeches and pro-BJP content, appeared during the election period. The Election Commission eventually ordered that political content without the required certification be removed, after opposition parties complained.

The larger democratic question is therefore not simply whether the ECI sometimes acts.

It is whether it acts consistently, promptly and without fear or favour.

Because democracy does not merely depend on voting.

It depends on whether every contestant believes that the rules will be enforced equally.

When an opposition leader faces immediate scrutiny while allegations involving those in power appear to move slowly—or disappear into institutional silence—the damage is larger than any individual complaint.

It begins to erode something much more precious:

public trust in the referee.

And once citizens stop believing that the electoral referee is neutral, the ballot box itself begins to carry the weight of suspicion.

The Election Commission therefore owes the country more than decisions.

It owes us transparency about the decisions—and equal accountability for everyone who seeks power.

Ukrainian winter: how bad could it get?

It’s pretty clear that Russian President Vladimir Putin will attempt to destroy what is left of Ukraine’s power sector this winter. In fact, the campaign has already started: last year’s bombardment got under way in September; this year’s arguably already started at the end of July.

Russia is increasingly targeting energy and power assets. Not that you’d notice as Bankova, Ukraine’s presidential administration, is focusing on the residential strikes and tragic loss of life in Kyiv as entire families are being killed every day.

Of course, this is perfectly understandable as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy is hoping to guilt-trip reluctant allies into giving him desperately needed interceptors and more resources. While Kyiv features prominently in the “Russia is a terrorist state” headlines, the real focus of the war is in Odesa and the Fortress Belt cities of the Donbas and the important casualties are DTEK and Naftogaz – though of course I don’t want to belittle the horrible civilian casualties’ reports.

However, I'm surprised at how little detailed reporting there is on just how much damage the power sector has taken since the war started. In 2022, Ukraine had about 59GW of installed capacity, (of which 22GW was thermal, 28GW hydro and 13.8GW was nuclear).

Going into last year’s winter campaign, Ukraine only had 14GW left with a winter demand of around 17GW. In a rare, detailed comment on the sector Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said yesterday that every single one of Ukraine’s power stations has suffered some sort of damage.

There was about a 3GW deficit in generating capacity last year, but the Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal admitted that in the first half of this year another 2GW has been taken out so the deficit is now on the order of 5GW.

And that is before the Russian winter bombardment has got going. Putin is reportedly stockpiling missiles after missile production capacity doubled last year and according to reports the full year production targets have already been hit. Mr P is not mucking about. This year’s attack is going to be devastating.

You’ll notice that the remain capacity is about the same as the nuclear power plant (NPP) generating capacity as obviously Russia can’t blow up the likes of Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant (ZNPP) as would cause an off-the-scale environmental disaster and, more importantly, almost certainly wreck Moscow’s relationship with Beijing, which has been pretty clear on its ban on doing anything nuclear.

But that doesn’t mean nuclear power will stay on the grid. As we reported last autumn, Russia also has the option of taking out the ultra-high voltage 750kV substations – pay attention as I'm sure you will be hearing a lot more about these after the summer is over.

These are especially large substations and are in effect the backbone of the Ukrainian grid. So far, Russia has largely ignored them, as part of Putin’s use of war as a political tool to try and force Zelenskiy to capitulate, but when it took out Odesa's substation last October it plunged the entire region into darkness for a week. As they are a Soviet-legacy piece of infrastructure, they are also very hard to repair or replace as no one makes parts for them.

Now imagine if Russia uses its highly accurate, and now unstoppable, ballistic missiles to target the substations. Even if only half of them were destroyed, bringing Ukraine’s available generation capacity down to 6GW that would blow out the power deficit to over 10GW – an impossible gap to close. And Shmyhal said last week, Bankova is afraid that Russia will also target water and sewage infrastructure. You can live in an apartment with -10°C indoor temperatures – many Kyivian residents did it last year by putting up tents in their living rooms  – but how long can you live without running water or working toilets?

Once you start digging into the details you can see why Zelenskiy is starting to look so desperate. There is very little he can do to stop it. US President Donald Trump has flip flopped on the Patriot licensing rights, which is reportedly being blocked by the leading US arms makers who are afraid of losing their profits to Ukraine (!).

There are also several hundred interceptors in Europe (remember Zelenskiy also asked Trump for 300 to get through the winter), but as we reported, and Politicoconfirmed last week, those European governments are refusing to give them up – Spain and Greece in particular which have the most.

Greece is not turning out to be a good friend of Ukraine’s, is it? Athens also blocked the 21stsanctions package until it got an exemption from the oil price cap sanctions and Greek tankers just exported a record amount of oil from Russia, helping to fill the Kremlin’s war coffers… And they said Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban was a good friend of Russia’s.

Trump was also badgered into promising to send Ukraine interceptor missiles “every month”. But no one has put a number on that. I strongly suspect the Pentagon is only intending to send new ones as they roll off the conveyor belt – about five a month – so at least keep its depleted stockpile stable. Given Russia is capable of firing five ballistic missiles a day that is not going to make any difference at all. Russia fired an estimated 900 missiles (not counting drones) at Ukraine last year, according to Center for Strategic & International Studies (CSIS). This year that number could easily double.

Another detail that is not getting enough attention is just how much damage Ukraine’s long distance “sanctions” (as Zelenskiy refers to drone strikes now) actually do to Russia’s refineries. But this is more excusable, as obviously neither the Kremlin nor the companies are keen to share this information. But what is becoming clear is that as the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) switches targets from oil refineries to warehouses, many of Russia’s circa 35 refineries that have been hit – and all of them have now been hit – are affecting repairs and at least partially coming back online. The fuel crisis has clearly passed peak and petrol stations are starting to open again. That is also partly thanks to supplies coming from Belarus, Kazakhstan and especially India.

India is another one that has turned out to be especially chummy with the Kremlin, but you can understand that too. As an ex-colony, it has not been particularly well treated by the Trump administration and has a growing resentment for the Western neo-colonial treatment it still gets whenever it goes to the West for help, like in last year’s short war with Pakistan.

Meduza had an interesting go at assessing the damage to Russian refineries by referring to infrared satellite maps in an article today, which concluded what was already assumed: Ukrainian drones are not powerful enough to destroy refineries, but can do serious damage to some of their more sensitive equipment that puts them out of action for months. But the bottom line is, Ukraine doesn’t have the destructive firepower to collapse the Russian economy or force Putin into negotiations in a position of weakness.

So, what does Ukraine with only 6GW in the depths of winter look like? It’s hard to say definitely, especially given the Ukrainian population managed to tough out last year’s attempt to freeze it into submission, but we are probably talking about an electricity emergency approaching a humanitarian crisis, particularly in the large cities.

Ukrainian winter peak electricity demand has been around 16.5–18GW, and the IEA says a cold winter can push demand to 18GW or more. So, 6GW of available/operational generation capacity would cover only roughly one-third of unconstrained peak demand. Even adding the present 2.1GW winter import capability from the EU would leave Ukraine with perhaps 8.1GW against demand of 18GW – about half of what is needed.

The state would be forced to ration electricity heavily and protect critical loads: hospitals, water and sewage pumping (if they are not destroyed too), telecommunications, military facilities, railways, district-heating systems and other essential infrastructure. Households and ordinary businesses would absorb a disproportionate share of extensive rolling blackouts that could extend to 12-18 hours a day for residential.

And that assumes the substations survive. If they are knocked out then the blackouts will be complete and could last for days or even weeks.

Electricity itself isn't necessarily the greatest danger. The lack of heat and water are. One of the big dangers is that if the power to a building is gone, you have to turn the water off, even if Russia doesn’t target the pumping stations, otherwise the water will freeze and burst their pipes – serious damage that can’t be repaired until spring, when the whole system has to be rebuilt.

Where is the cut off? Last year residents could cope with 6–10-hour daily blackouts. With 12–18-hour blackouts you get serious economic and social disruption, but there are some work arounds like generators. However, with only 2–6 hours of electricity per day the cities will begin to be unliveable as apartments become too cold to inhabit and things like water have to be shut off completely and drained from the buildings. Those who can, will leave the city for the dacha or leave the country. Iuliia Mendel, Zelenskiy’s former press secretary, has already reported on traffic jams at the borders as some people are already leaving in anticipation of what might come.

I'm not saying this will happen. Ukrainians have demonstrated extraordinary resilience and the ability to function through last year’s blackouts. But this is a very real scenario that is lurking behind Zelenskiy's frenetic diplomatic outreach at the moment. Ukraine is not ready to repel a large Russian missile bombardment and its partners are either unwilling, but mostly, unable to do much to help it at this point.

@Elonmusk, regarding relevancy and shadow banning: 

I think you should let the populace block who they don’t want to listen to, and not the algorithm actively blocking you, because 200–500 active accounts did, even if they may be bots or paid users. 

This then creates a negative incentive to harm and harass others if you have the numbers. If this is a public square, let it be one. 

If there’s a man on the street with a sign, only those who choose to pay attention see him; but when the negative incentive is applied, he exists, but others don’t see him. 

So, personal active blocking is more accurate to the public square you talk about—that’s actually free.

 I mean, porn sites are still accessible because of personal choice, no matter how much a large proportion of the population speak negatively  of them because they’re largely a personal choice.

For instance, WhatsApp status posts or chats are not tampered with. If I hide anything, it stays hidden for me and only me. So first the system needs to respect individual taste by simply letting people choose and block who they don’t want to see.

 Only after that should it start showing what users are actually interested in. Right now it feels like the platform is controlling what people see, not for protection, but to keep information away from them.

Looking at the most recent public algorithm (xai-org/x-algorithm), the exact places that need fixing are clear. The Phoenix model predicts how likely someone is to block, mute, report, or hit “not interested.”

RankingScorer then multiplies those predictions by heavy negative weights (report around –234, mute around –58.8, not interested around –43.2, block around –31.2).

Real reports and blocks also feed into labeling systems and visibility filters that can bury posts more widely, especially for people who don’t follow the author.

That’s how a relatively small group can tank reach and create the incentive to harass. 

The hard personal filter already in the code — AuthorSocialgraphFilter — is the right piece. It just removes posts from accounts you blocked or muted. 

Everything that predicts negatives ahead of time or turns other people’s actions into reduced visibility for everyone else is the problem.

Here’s how a real public square that can’t be controlled by any government or body would actually work. It would be run only by the people who individually choose to listen or not.

Start with individual taste as the foundation. Let every user block or mute whoever/ideas they don’t want to see. 

Those choices stay local/user. The algorithm then learns your preferences — both positive and negative — only from what you do: likes, replies, time spent, shares, follows, and also hides, mutes, blocks, and “not interested.” From that it builds a Preferences feed that matches your taste. 

Other people’s reports don’t get to decide what shows up for you.
Then give people clean, separate views they control:

•  A pure Following feed that only shows posts from the people you chose to follow.

•  A Similar-to-Following layer that brings in accounts and posts that feel like the ones you already follow.

•  Exploration modes you turn on when you want them: mainstream or trending, and location views (India, Nigeria, Australia or cities like , Benin, Toronto). 

These stay separate and still respect your blocks and mutes. They don’t quietly leak into your other feeds.

Add real transparency on reputation. Instead of an invisible algorithm quietly burying posts because of hidden reports, put a public reputation section on each post. 

Anyone can see it’s been reported, how many times, and the stated reasons. The original poster gets a clear public space to respond and defend it. 

Reputation and ranking then rise or fall based on what people can actually read and judge for themselves. 

Coordinated or fake reports become visible and easy to challenge. Good defenses become visible too. The public decides.

Under this setup no outside body can quietly control the square. The only way a voice disappears from your view is if you remove it. 

There’s no payoff for mass-reporting someone just to shut them up. Visibility is the default.

Suppression is personal and explicit. Your feed learns from your own + and – signals. 

Exploration is something you choose.

Reputation is a 2 sided sword.

This platform is greatly improved thanks to you, but it’s still shying away from true nature which is sovereignty from the state.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

On the night of 14th August 1947, a flag flew on Jawaharlal Nehru's car as it went over Raisina Hill. It was the first time the tricolour we know today was ever flown.

That flag had been stitched under the supervision of a 28 year old woman.

Her name was Surayya Tyabji.

She was born in 1919 in Hyderabad. She was a painter. Her work was later shown in London and in Jakarta. She was married to Badruddin Tyabji, a civil servant who was part of the group working on what independent India would look like.

Everyone had assumed the flag was settled. Pingali Venkayya had designed the tricolour used by the Congress, with Gandhi's charkha in the middle. It had been carried through the freedom movement for over 20 years.

Then, weeks before independence, a problem was raised. That flag was a party flag. A country that was about to include everyone could not fly the symbol of one political party.

So the design had to be redone, quickly.

The Tyabjis were given the job.

They replaced the charkha with the Ashoka Chakra, the wheel from the Lion Capital of Ashoka at Sarnath. The reason was simple and deliberate. Ashoka belonged to all Indians, and to no party.

Their daughter Laila Tyabji has written the family's account of it. Her mother drew the graphic version. The printing press at the Viceregal Lodge made the impressions. Everyone approved.

The English historian Trevor Royle recorded in his book that the flag which flew on Nehru's car that night had been made by Tyabji's wife.

On 22nd July 1947 the design was accepted by the Constituent Assembly.

A report in the Times of India in January 1950 described that first flag as having been presented to the nation by the women of India at the midnight session of the Constituent Assembly on 14th August 1947.

Before the flag, the same couple had worked on the national emblem. Nehru asked Badruddin to do something about it because he had an eye for these things. Surayya drew the version of the 4 lions that has been on every Indian government document since.

She was 28 years old.

She died in 1978 in Mumbai.

Her daughter has said that neither of her parents ever felt they had designed the national emblem. They felt they had only reminded India of something that had always been part of its identity.

Official records of the Constituent Assembly do not name individual contributors, so most textbooks still credit only Venkayya, and his work genuinely came first.

But today, when the flag goes up, look at the wheel in the middle of it.

A young Muslim woman put it there, on purpose, so that no Indian would be left out of it.

IFF’s Statement on the Blocking of X Account of the Cockroach Janta Party

22 May 2026

On May 21, 2026, the X (formerly Twitter) handle of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) (@CJP_2029) was withheld in India under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. IFF strongly condemns the blocking of the CJP’s X handle as a blatant misuse of State power and an arbitrary and disproportionate attempt to stifle freedom of speech and expression, a fundamental right guaranteed under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution of India.

According to reporting by The Indian Express on May 22, 2026, the blocking directions were issued on the basis of inputs from the Intelligence Bureau citing threat to the sovereignty of India, jeopardizing national security and the fact that the account was gaining traction among young people. Section 69A of the IT Act, 2000, empowers the Central government to direct any Government agency or intermediary to block public access to information in the “interest of sovereignty and integrity of India, defence of India, security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States or public order or for preventing incitement to the commission of any cognizable offence”. While Section 69A of the IT Act, 2000 permits blocking on limited grounds, these grounds cannot be vague and speculative. Political commentary and criticism of public institutions are protected forms of speech under the Indian Constitution. The popularity of the account or the fact that the account mobilised young people through political expression cannot by itself be treated as a threat to national security.

The Indian Express’s report mentions that “blocking orders are issued under a confidential framework” which is deeply concerning. We remind the Union Government that the Supreme Court of India upheld Section 69A of the IT Act, 2000 in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) on the basis that it is a narrowly drawn provision with several safeguards in place, including written reasoning for the blocking that is subject to legal challenge. State censorship like the blocking of CJP’s X account propagates opacity and provides affected users with no options for redressal, thereby effectively defeating these safeguards. IFF calls on the Union government to ensure timely notices are provided to affected users along with clear grounds and avenues for remedy.

IFF has previously explained how users whose constitutional rights are being infringed upon by the State can seek restoration of their blocked content. If you are an Indian social media user or journalist whose content has been blocked due to a government order, please write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in.

Every piece of content online is more than just a post. It captures a moment, shares information, and brings conversations to people who might never have heard them otherwise.

It’s time to raise your voice louder than ever. Speak up against censorship. If your content has been taken down, report it to https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s RightsLine at rightsline@sflc.in.

Not every message is what it seems. 🛑

A message might look like it’s from someone you know, a company you trust, or even a familiar system. But fraudsters can use fake messages and caller IDs to trick you into sharing information or giving them access.

So, before you respond, take a moment to check the message header.

Businesses sending commercial messages are assigned a unique Header ID. Checking the header can help you identify who the message is actually from and spot potential scams.

You can find the list of allotted Header IDs here: https://t.co/7IP5mAjPiR

quotedTweet.text:
IFF has written to the Union Home Secretary and the Census Commissioner over the household survey notified four days ago. Serial numbers 36 to 40 ask for mobile, Aadhaar, voter ID and passport numbers, not whether you have them, unlike serial number 40, which only asks about availability of a driving license.

IFF supports enumerating caste for substantive equality. But pairing Aadhaar numbers with religion and caste sits against the Aadhaar Act's bar on profiling, and the questionnaire itself remains unpublished.
We are not opposed to the census. We want it conducted in a way that earns public trust.

text: Yes, IFF unambiguously supports caste enumeration within a census exercise as it advances the goal of substantive equality in the design of state welfare programmes. Our concerns are limited to directly PII (Aadhaar numbers) and lack of data protection and safety safeguards.

Other countries have adopted stronger safeguards. UN census principles emphasise that individual information should not be linked to other government databases for non-statistical purposes. Countries including Canada and Australia avoid collecting certain identifiers or keep contact information separate from statistical data. Germany’s Constitutional Court has also rejected census-to-register linkage. (7/8)

IFF supports the inclusion of caste in Census 2027. Reliable caste data can be essential to understanding inequality and advancing constitutional commitments to equality. But counting caste does not require creating identity-linked records. We have asked the government to delete unnecessary identifiers, guarantee that data will not be linked with other databases, publish security and retention safeguards, and make any retained fields expressly voluntary. (8/8)

According to @imsoumyarendra  of the @IndianExpress, data accessed by the newspaper shows that between March and July 2026, the Central Government sent close to 1,95,000 blocking/removal directions to Instagram, Facebook and YouTube, an average of one order every 68 seconds, or about 1,275 a day. Instagram alone accounted for over half of these orders, much of it during the period of the Delhi students' protests against exam leaks.

We had filed an RTI seeking exactly this kind of information: the total number of blocking/removal directions issued through the Sahyog portal, a month wise and platform wise break up, the legal provisions invoked, and the authorities issuing them.
Read the whole report: https://t.co/px9q8AA1oB
